states: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
guidance_disclaimer: General public-health information summarised from the cited source. It is not medical advice and not specific to any location: follow the protocols of NCDC/IDSP and the State Health Department.

Dengue.transmission: Spread by the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, which bite mainly in the daytime and breed in clean standing water in and around homes.
Dengue.prevention: Empty, cover or scrub water-holding containers every week; use repellents, window screens and clothing that covers arms and legs.
Dengue.response: Intensify mosquito breeding-source reduction around reported cases and make sure clinics watch for warning signs of severe dengue. There is no specific antiviral; care is supportive, and aspirin and ibuprofen should be avoided.
Dengue.source_name: WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue

Chikungunya.transmission: Spread by the same day-biting Aedes mosquitoes that transmit dengue.
Chikungunya.prevention: Remove standing water where mosquitoes breed and prevent daytime bites with repellents, screens and covering clothing.
Chikungunya.response: Source reduction around cases and supportive care for fever and joint pain; there is no specific antiviral treatment.

Malaria.transmission: Spread by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, which bite mainly between dusk and dawn.
Malaria.prevention: Sleep under insecticide-treated nets; indoor residual spraying in affected areas.
Malaria.response: Test every suspected case (rapid test or microscopy) and treat confirmed cases promptly according to the national drug policy.

Cholera.transmission: Caused by eating food or drinking water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae.
Cholera.prevention: Safe drinking water (chlorinated or boiled), sanitation and handwashing with soap; oral cholera vaccine in hotspots.
Cholera.response: Give oral rehydration solution immediately; severe dehydration needs intravenous fluids and antibiotics. Find and treat the contaminated water source.

Acute Diarrheal Disease.transmission: Usually spread through water or food contaminated with faeces, and from person to person where hygiene is poor.
Acute Diarrheal Disease.prevention: Safe drinking water, improved sanitation, handwashing with soap, and rotavirus vaccination for infants.
Acute Diarrheal Disease.response: Rehydrate with ORS, with zinc supplements for children; test and disinfect the suspected water source.

Food Poisoning.transmission: Caused by food contaminated with bacteria, viruses, parasites, toxins or chemicals; it does not spread between districts.
Food Poisoning.prevention: WHO's five keys to safer food: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, use safe water and raw materials.
Food Poisoning.response: Identify and withdraw the implicated food, collect food and stool samples, and rehydrate those affected.

Measles.transmission: A highly contagious airborne virus spread by coughing, sneezing and close contact.
Measles.prevention: Two doses of measles-containing vaccine for every child.
Measles.response: Outbreak-response vaccination, isolation of cases, and two doses of vitamin A, 24 hours apart, for children with measles.

Rubella.transmission: Spread by airborne droplets when infected people cough or sneeze.
Rubella.response: Infection in early pregnancy can cause miscarriage or congenital rubella syndrome: protect and follow up pregnant contacts.

Hepatitis / Jaundice.transmission: Outbreaks of jaundice are usually hepatitis A or E, spread by the faecal-oral route through contaminated water or food.
Hepatitis / Jaundice.prevention: Safe drinking water, proper sewage disposal and hand hygiene; hepatitis A vaccine where recommended.
Hepatitis / Jaundice.response: Test and chlorinate water supplies. Hepatitis E is particularly dangerous in pregnancy, so refer pregnant women with jaundice early.
Hepatitis / Jaundice.source_name: WHO fact sheets: Hepatitis A and Hepatitis E

Typhoid.transmission: Caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread through contaminated food and water.
Typhoid.prevention: Safe water, sanitation and food hygiene; typhoid conjugate vaccine.
Typhoid.response: Treat with antibiotics guided by local resistance patterns, which are worsening, and trace the contaminated source.

Mumps.transmission: Spread by respiratory droplets and direct contact with an infected person.
Mumps.response: Isolate cases while infectious; care is supportive.

Chickenpox.transmission: Spreads easily from people with chickenpox to anyone who has not had the disease or the vaccine. A person is contagious from 1 to 2 days before the rash appears until all the blisters have crusted over.
Chickenpox.prevention: Chickenpox (varicella) vaccine; keep cases away from school, work and vulnerable people until every blister has crusted over.
Chickenpox.response: Most cases need only supportive care. Antiviral medicine is recommended for people at higher risk of serious illness, who should see a healthcare provider early.

Rabies.transmission: Spread by the bite or scratch of an infected animal, most often a dog. It does not spread between districts on its own.
Rabies.prevention: Vaccinate dogs and avoid contact with stray or wild animals.
Rabies.response: After any bite: wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes and start post-exposure vaccination at once, with rabies immunoglobulin when indicated. Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms begin.

Leptospirosis.transmission: Caught through contact with water or soil contaminated by the urine of infected animals, especially rodents, often after flooding.
Leptospirosis.prevention: Avoid wading in floodwater, wear protective footwear and control rodents.
Leptospirosis.response: Treat early with antibiotics; alert clinicians to fever cases after floods.

Acute Encephalitis Syndrome / JE.transmission: Japanese encephalitis is spread by Culex mosquitoes, with pigs and water birds as the main hosts of the virus.
Acute Encephalitis Syndrome / JE.prevention: JE vaccination in endemic districts and protection from mosquito bites, especially at dusk and at night.
Acute Encephalitis Syndrome / JE.response: There is no antiviral treatment: refer suspected cases quickly for supportive hospital care.

Diphtheria.transmission: Spread by respiratory droplets and close contact.
Diphtheria.prevention: Diphtheria-containing vaccine with all recommended booster doses.
Diphtheria.response: Give diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics without waiting for laboratory confirmation; trace close contacts for antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccination.

Nipah.transmission: Passed to people from fruit bats (for example through contaminated fruit or raw date-palm sap) or pigs, and from person to person through close contact.
Nipah.prevention: Do not drink raw date-palm sap; wash and peel fruit; use gloves and masks when caring for the sick.
Nipah.response: Isolate suspected cases, trace contacts and apply strict infection control. There is no specific treatment; care is supportive.

Zika Virus.transmission: Spread mainly by Aedes mosquitoes; also from mother to fetus and through sexual contact.
Zika Virus.prevention: Prevent mosquito bites and remove breeding sites; pregnant women need particular protection.
Zika Virus.response: Infection in pregnancy can cause microcephaly and other birth defects: follow up pregnant women in affected areas.

Mpox.transmission: Spread by close contact with an infected person's skin lesions or body fluids, or with contaminated materials.
Mpox.prevention: Avoid close physical contact with people who have mpox; vaccination for those at risk, according to national policy.
Mpox.response: Isolate cases until lesions have healed and monitor their contacts.

Influenza.transmission: Spread by respiratory droplets when infected people cough or sneeze.
Influenza.prevention: Annual vaccination for high-risk groups; hand hygiene and covering coughs.
Influenza.response: Antiviral treatment for severe illness and for people at high risk of complications.

Scrub Typhus.transmission: Spread by the bite of infected chiggers (larval mites) found in scrub vegetation. It does not spread from person to person.
Scrub Typhus.prevention: No vaccine exists: avoid areas of heavy scrub, use insect repellent and wear protective clothing.
Scrub Typhus.response: Treat early with doxycycline, without waiting for laboratory confirmation when suspicion is high.
